title: Verbi Seguiti da Preposizione + Infinito
subtitle: Which verbs need a, which need di, and which need nothing at all before an infinitive.
objectives: Group common verbs by whether they take a, di, or no preposition before an infinitive
Apply the pattern correctly in context
Recognize a handful of high-frequency exceptions worth memorizing individually

content.intro: There's no single rule for predicting which preposition (if any) connects a verb to a following infinitive — but the most common verbs sort into learnable groups.
content.explanation: Modal verbs (dovere, potere, volere) and a handful of others take the bare infinitive with no preposition, as you already know. Many verbs of movement and beginning take a; many verbs of stopping, deciding, and trying take di. There's real overlap and no fully reliable shortcut — building intuition through exposure is the realistic goal at this stage.

rules.heading: a) No preposition
rules.body: dovere, potere, volere, sapere, piacere, preferire, amare, desiderare: Preferisco restare a casa.

rules.heading: b) + a
rules.body: andare a, venire a, cominciare a, iniziare a, imparare a, continuare a, riuscire a, aiutare a: Ho imparato a nuotare da bambino.

rules.heading: c) + di
rules.body: finire di, smettere di, decidere di, cercare di, dimenticare di, avere bisogno di, avere voglia di, chiedere di, promettere di: Ho deciso di cambiare lavoro.

examples.it: Ho smesso di fumare due anni fa.
examples.en: I quit smoking two years ago.

examples.it: Sto imparando a suonare la chitarra.
examples.en: I'm learning to play the guitar.
It's kept raining since this morning.

examples.it: Ho bisogno di riposare un po'.
examples.en: I need to rest a bit.

commonMistakes.why: Smettere requires di before an infinitive — it's never dropped.
Imparare takes a, not di, before an infinitive.
Volere, a modal verb, takes no preposition at all before an infinitive.

items.explanation: Avere bisogno takes di before an infinitive.

summary: Modal-type verbs take no preposition; many motion/beginning verbs take a; many stopping/deciding verbs take di.
There's real overlap — treat each verb's pattern as a fact to learn alongside its meaning.
The preposition, once required, is never optional or interchangeable.
